title: Flying Home for Diwali and Chhath: 72% of Travellers Say Fares Are Higher This Year
excerpt: A 19,993-person survey finds most festive flyers paying more than in 2025, with Patna-bound tickets for November 7 at Rs 17,000-28,000 as fuel surcharges and tight capacity compound the rush.
body:
• A LocalCircles survey released October 12 found 72% of travellers flying home for the festivals are paying more than in 2025; 54% are paying over 50% extra and 9% more than double.
  • Fares to Patna for November 7 run Rs 17,000 to Rs 28,000 one-way from major metros, up to three times usual levels, with Delhi-Patna at Rs 17,000-20,000.
  • Higher jet fuel prices, new fuel surcharges of Rs 400-1,200 on domestic tickets from October 9, and reduced capacity are compounding concentrated festive demand.
  • Reader check: return legs from Bihar after the rush are far cheaper - Darbhanga departures run Rs 5,000-9,000 - and fares are expected to ease after November 20, so shifting dates or splitting bookings can cut the total materially.

Flying home for Diwali and Chhath this year costs substantially more than last year for most travellers in India. A LocalCircles survey released on October 12, covering 19,993 air travellers across 277 districts, found that 72% of respondents travelling to their hometowns for the festive season are paying more for flights than in 2025, according to India Today. More than half, 54%, said they were paying over 50% extra, and 9% said fares had more than doubled.

The sharpest pressure is on routes into Bihar ahead of Diwali on November 8 and Chhath on November 15, when workers in Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and other metros travel home in a compressed window. Fare listings for November 7 show one-way tickets to Patna between Rs 17,000 and Rs 28,000 depending on origin - roughly three times normal levels on several sectors.

What the fares look like

Delhi-Patna, normally one of the busiest festive routes, is priced at Rs 17,000 to Rs 20,000 for November 7, with Air India listing Rs 19,048 and IndiGo Rs 18,291. Ahmedabad-Patna is the most expensive of the major sectors at Rs 25,000 to Rs 28,000, followed by Bengaluru-Patna at Rs 22,000 to Rs 24,000, Chennai-Patna at Rs 21,000 to Rs 23,000 and Mumbai-Patna at Rs 20,000 to Rs 22,000, according to the fare details compiled by Patna Press. Officials cited in that report warned fares could reach four times normal levels on some routes as the festival dates approach, before easing after November 20.

The pattern is asymmetric. Return journeys out of Bihar after the festivals are priced far lower, because demand flows one way. On the Darbhanga routes, for example, outbound tickets from Mumbai have crossed Rs 30,000 while returns to Mumbai are available at Rs 7,000 to Rs 9,000.

Why fares are climbing together

Demand alone does not explain the scale of the increase. Aviation turbine fuel for domestic airlines rose by about Rs 16 per litre from October 1, to around Rs 137 per litre - the third consecutive monthly increase - and fuel accounts for roughly 40% of airline operating costs. Airlines have passed part of that through directly: after IndiGo moved first, Air India, Air India Express and Akasa Air imposed fuel surcharges of Rs 400 to Rs 1,200 per domestic ticket, by distance slab, on bookings made from October 9.

Capacity is the other constraint. Reports on the festive market cite reduced domestic flight capacity alongside the fuel increases, which leaves fewer seats to absorb the Diwali-Chhath surge. The shortage of confirmed train tickets on the same routes pushes still more travellers toward flights, according to officials quoted by Patna Press.

What it means if you are still booking

The practical levers are dates and direction. Fares are expected to normalise after November 20, so travellers who can arrive after the peak or leave later avoid the worst pricing. Comparing the full trip cost - baggage, transfers and the return leg - matters more than the headline fare, a point made in festive budget guidance published alongside the survey. For diaspora travellers connecting through Delhi or Mumbai onto a domestic leg to Bihar, Bengal or Odisha, the domestic segment is now the expensive part of the journey: booking the connection on off-peak dates, or holding the return for after November 20, can save more than any single fare sale.

What happens next

The government has said it will not impose a hard cap on festive fares but is advising airlines to keep rates reasonable during the peak. With Diwali three weeks away and Chhath a week after, the next fare moves will be set by how quickly remaining seats sell. Travellers who have not booked should expect prices to firm, not soften, into early November.
